reasons: Only the top of the file is visible, so login and permission logic cannot be checked.

terms.meaning: A signed piece of text that proves who a user is, given after login.
A method for storing passwords as scrambled hashes, so the real password is never saved.
A fixed scrambled form of a value, which cannot be turned back into the original.
A written rule that says what shape and types the data must have.
A library that checks data against a schema.
Code that runs between an incoming request and the final handler, often to check access.
A label, such as admin or analyst, that decides what a user may do.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports for login and checks
sections.what: Brings in the web types, the token library, the password hashing library, and the validation library.
sections.why: The imports show that the file handles login tokens, password checks, and input validation.
sections.watch_out: Token and password behavior depends on these libraries, so upgrades can change how logins work.

sections.name: authUserSchema, authUsersSchema
sections.title: Shape of user accounts
sections.what: Each user needs a subject name, a password hash, and a role of admin or analyst. The user list must contain at least one user.
sections.why: Likely reason: rejects a malformed user list early, before logins are attempted.
sections.watch_out: The schema only checks the password hash is text, so a plain text password would also pass. Any new role must be added to the allowed list.

sections.name: loadAuthUsers
sections.title: Reads and checks the user list
sections.what: Reads the AUTH_USERS setting, which must be a JSON list of users, checks its shape, and returns the list. The server refuses to start if the setting is missing, is not valid JSON, or has the wrong shape.
sections.why: Stops the app from running with no working login list.
sections.watch_out: The list is kept in memory after first load, so changes to the setting need a server restart to take effect.

sections.name: getJwtSecret
sections.title: Gets the token signing key
sections.what: Reads the secret used to sign login tokens from JWT_SECRET, or from SESSION_SECRET if that is the only one set, and requires at least 32 characters.
sections.why: Likely reason: a short signing key is easier to guess, so the length is enforced.
sections.watch_out: If neither setting is present or the value is too short, the server will not start.

sections.name: SYSTEM_SUBS
sections.title: Accounts allowed without a user entry
sections.what: Lists account names that may use a validly signed token without appearing in the user list. It includes verify-script by default, plus any names given in SYSTEM_SUBS.
sections.why: The comments say this lets automated checks call protected endpoints without a human account.
sections.watch_out: Any name in SYSTEM_SUBS gets access with a valid token and has no user entry, so keep that list short and reviewed.

sections.name: buildAuthSubjects
sections.title: Collects the known usernames
sections.what: Builds a set of every username in the user list so that membership can be checked quickly.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fast lookup is simpler than searching the list on each request.

sections.name: validateAuthConfig
sections.title: Checks login setup at startup
sections.what: Exported function that loads the user list, the signing key and the username set in one step, so bad configuration fails at startup.
sections.why: Likely reason: fail at boot rather than on the first login attempt.
sections.watch_out: It only protects the app if the startup code actually calls it.

sections.name: getAuthUsers
sections.title: Returns the user list
sections.what: Returns the loaded user list, loading it first if startup did not.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond acting as a fallback to startup loading.

sections.name: getAuthSubjects
sections.title: Returns the known usernames
sections.what: Returns the set of usernames, building it from the user list if needed. Protected requests use it to reject tokens for unknown users.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond supporting the per-request subject check.

sections.name: getSecret
sections.title: Returns the signing key
sections.what: Returns the token signing key, loading it first if it has not been loaded yet.
sections.why: Same first-use loading pattern as the user list.

sections.name: AuthUser
sections.title: Shape of the logged-in user
sections.what: Describes the user attached to each request: a username and a role that is either admin or analyst. It also tells TypeScript that requests can carry this user.
sections.why: Lets route code read the caller's role safely.
sections.watch_out: The role is a fixed pair of values, so a new role must be added here as well as wherever it is checked.

sections.name: loginAttempts
sections.title: Stores login attempt counts
sections.what: Keeps an in-memory record of login attempts per IP address, including when each 15-minute window started.
sections.why: Supports the login limit that slows down password guessing.
sections.watch_out: The record lives only in memory and is never cleaned up, so restarts reset all counts and multiple server copies do not share them.

sections.name: checkLoginRateLimit
sections.title: Limits login tries per address
sections.what: Allows at most 5 login attempts per IP address in each 15-minute window and returns false once that limit is passed.
sections.watch_out: Every attempt counts, including successful ones, so users who share one address can lock each other out.

sections.name: handleLogin
sections.title: Login endpoint and dev bypass switch
sections.what: Handles login. It checks the address limit, requires a username and password, compares the password with a stored hash, and returns a token valid for 24 hours. It also defines AUTH_DISABLED, a development-only switch that skips login checks and is ignored in production.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps login rules in one place, and the switch lets local work continue without logins.
sections.watch_out: When the username is unknown the password check is skipped, so response time may reveal which usernames exist.

sections.name: requireAuth
sections.title: Checks the login token on requests
sections.what: Guards protected routes. It reads the Bearer token, verifies its signature and expiry, confirms the subject is a known user or an allowed system name, and attaches the user to the request. With AUTH_DISABLED on, every request is treated as admin.
sections.why: Keeps every protected route checked the same way.
sections.watch_out: The role comes from the token, not the current user list, so a role change only applies after that user logs in again, up to 24 hours later.

sections.name: requireRole
sections.title: Limits routes to certain roles
sections.what: Returns a check that lets a request through only when its role is in the allowed list. It answers 401 when there is no user and 403 when the role is not allowed.
sections.why: Lets a route restrict itself to admins or other specific roles.
sections.watch_out: It must run after the login check, otherwise requests are refused as unauthorized.

summary: Controls who can log in and which pages they can reach, using signed login tokens and password hashes.
purpose: Protects the API so only known users with valid accounts can use it, and limits some actions to admin users.
why: Reason not stated in the visible code. The shapes of user records are defined at the top, which suggests the file checks users when it starts.
how: Only the imports and the user record shape are visible. The shape requires a subject name, a password hash, and a role. The rest of the file, including login, token checks, and role checks, is not shown and cannot be explained here.
inputs: The user account list (from configuration) when it loads, and login requests in the rest of the file.
outputs: Not visible in the shown code.
risks: The schema checks only that a password hash is text, so a plain text password would also pass this check. Security-related logic is not visible, so its safety cannot be judged here.
debug: If startup fails with a user list problem, check that the list has at least one user and each user has a subject, a password hash, and a role of admin or analyst.
